q: One app server is at 90% CPU. Plan A: move it to a machine with four times the cores. Plan B: run four copies behind a load balancer. Which statement is right?
options: A is simpler, but capped and a single point of failure
B is always better, since adding machines has no downside
A can grow forever, since a bigger machine can always be bought
They are equal, since both give four times the CPU
why: Scaling up keeps one machine, so the code needs no change, but machine sizes stop somewhere and one crash takes the site down. Scaling out adds capacity and redundancy, but needs a load balancer and servers that keep no local state.
wrong: B needs a load balancer, stateless servers and more moving parts. A bigger machine is often a sensible first step.
The largest machines have a limit, and cost rises steeply near the top.
Same CPU, different failure behaviour: with A one crash is an outage; with B the other copies keep serving.

q: This login code ran fine on one server. After a second copy is added behind a round-robin load balancer, users get logged out at random. What is the robust fix?
options: Switch the balancer to least connections so requests spread evenly
Add more copies until each user's requests keep landing on one
Keep sessions in a shared store or a signed token, not in memory
Pin users to one server with sticky sessions; that fully fixes it
why: Each process has its own sessions dict, so a session created on one server is unknown to the other. Keeping sessions in a store that all servers share (a cache server or the database), or in a signed token the client sends, lets any server handle any request.
wrong: Any algorithm still sends some requests to the server that did not create the session.
More copies make it worse: each new one is another server that does not know the session.
Sticky sessions hide the issue, but a user still loses the session when their server dies or is removed.

q: During a traffic spike, the team adds five web servers within a minute and removes three of them an hour later, and no user notices. What property of the web tier makes this safe?
options: Each server keeps its own users' sessions in memory, for speed
Servers keep no user state, so any one can serve any request
Stateless means the servers use no database, so nothing must sync
Every server holds a full copy of the database to answer on its own
why: When servers keep nothing about a user between requests, and sessions and data live in shared stores, a new server can take traffic at once and a removed one loses nothing. That is why stateless services are the usual basis for scaling out.
wrong: Then removing a server would log out its users. Local session state is what makes removal unsafe.
Stateless servers usually do use a database. The state lives there, outside the server process.
A database copy on every server would make writes and consistency hard. Servers share the data stores instead.

q: Three app servers sit behind a load balancer that runs health checks. Server B crashes. What do users see?
options: The site goes down until B is back, since users are tied to servers
Requests meant for B wait in the balancer until B restarts
Nothing at all: B's half-done requests are replayed on A and C
B fails its checks and gets no traffic; A and C keep serving
why: The balancer probes each server and stops routing to one that fails, so new requests go to A and C. Requests B was handling when it crashed may fail and need a retry, and A and C carry more load, but the site stays up.
wrong: Routing around a dead server is the balancer's job; A and C keep taking new requests.
The balancer routes around a failed server instead of waiting for it; that is the point of health checks.
Work in progress on B is usually lost. Clients may need to retry; the balancer only routes new requests.

q: Each request spends about 800 ms resizing an image on the app server's CPU, even when traffic is light. The team adds two more identical servers behind the load balancer. What changes?
options: More requests are handled at once, but each still takes about 800 ms
Each request now takes about 270 ms, a third of the time
Nothing, since load balancers only help with static files
Each request gets slower, since it must pass through all three servers
why: A load balancer sends each request to one server, which still does the full 800 ms of work. Three servers can work on three times as many requests in parallel, so throughput rises while the latency of a single request stays the same.
wrong: One request is not split across servers. The resize still runs on one CPU.
Balancers spread any kind of request across servers, dynamic work included.
Each request goes to exactly one server; the balancer adds only a small hop.

q: A store's database is slowing down under read traffic. Which data is the best first candidate for a cache in front of it?
options: Each account's balance, which changes on every payment and must be exact
The log of every click, written once and almost never read again
Product pages that thousands read and that change a few times a day
One-time login codes, each read once right after it is created
why: A cache pays off when the same data is read far more often than it changes, so most reads become hits. Product pages fit: many readers, rare changes, and a short delay before a change shows up is acceptable.
wrong: Data that changes constantly and must be exact is where stale cache entries hurt most.
Data that is rarely read gives almost no cache hits, so it only uses memory.
A value read once is never read from the cache again, so every read is a miss.

q: Three app servers each keep a local in-memory cache of prices with a 10-minute expiry. An admin's price update reaches server A, which updates the database and deletes its own entry. What follows?
options: Everyone sees the new price right away, since A cleared its entry
Users sent to B or C may see the old price for up to 10 minutes
Users on B and C get errors until their entries expire
Everyone, A's users included, keeps seeing the old price for 10 minutes
why: A's invalidation only touched A's memory. B and C still hold the old value and serve it until their copies expire. With scaled-out servers, a shared cache or a way to tell every server to drop the entry avoids this, or the delay must be acceptable.
wrong: Each server has its own cache. Deleting A's entry does nothing to the copies held by B and C.
A stale entry is still a valid value. It is served without any error, which is why stale data is easy to miss.
A deleted its entry, so its next read misses and loads the new price from the database.

q: This app uses the cache-aside pattern. During peak hours the cache server restarts and comes back empty. What happens next?
code:
def get_product(pid):
    item = cache.get(pid)
    if item is None:  # miss
        item = db.load_product(pid)
        cache.set(pid, item, ttl=300)
    return item
options: Reads fail until someone reloads the cache's contents from a backup copy
The cache refills itself from the database in the background
Users get the values cached before the restart for 5 minutes
Reads still work, but misses hit the database until the cache warms
why: In cache-aside the application owns the logic: on a miss it reads the database and fills the cache itself. An empty cache means a burst of misses, so the database briefly takes the full read load, but every request still gets an answer.
wrong: The database is the source of truth. The cache holds copies and can always be rebuilt from it.
In cache-aside the cache never loads data by itself. Entries return only as the app misses and fills them.
The restart wiped the entries. Nothing old is left to serve.

q: A site runs in one data center in Frankfurt. Users in Israel and Brazil say pages are slow, mostly while large images and script files load. What does a CDN help with here?
options: Serving those static files from servers near each user
Speeding up the database queries behind each page
Caching each user's private account page for everyone to reuse
Replacing the Frankfurt servers, which can then be shut down
why: A CDN keeps copies of static files (images, scripts, styles, video) on servers in many regions. Users download them from a nearby location, which cuts the distance travelled and takes that load off the origin servers.
wrong: A CDN caches files near users; it does not touch queries running in your database.
Private per-user pages must not be shared between users; CDNs fit content that is the same for everyone.
The CDN fetches from the origin when its copies are missing or expired, so the origin stays.

q: A sign-up handler calls a slow email provider (about 3 s) before it responds. The team puts an email job on a message queue, and a worker sends it. What improves?
options: Each email is delivered faster, since a queue speeds up the work itself
Sign-up returns without waiting, and bursts of emails wait in line
Emails can no longer fail, since the queue guarantees success
Nothing, since the user still waits for the worker to finish
why: The handler only adds a job to the queue, which is fast, and responds. A worker sends emails at its own pace, so a spike of sign-ups waits in the queue instead of slowing every request. The email takes as long as before; the user just does not wait for it.
wrong: The worker calls the same provider, so sending takes as long. Only the request stops waiting.
The provider can still fail. A queue makes retries easy, but a retried job may run twice, so it should be safe to repeat.
The handler responds right after adding the job; the worker runs separately, later.
